title: Git for Engineers: Atomic Commits and Evidence

questions.question: A single commit contains a fee-rounding fix, a retry loop around a bank upload, and a renamed config key. The retry loop causes a double payment. What is the cheapest safe way to remove just the retry loop?
options: Run git revert on the commit; Git reverts only the hunks that changed behaviour
There is none; the commit must be split by hand because revert undoes all three changes
Run git reset --hard to the previous commit on main and force-push the result
Run git bisect to isolate the retry loop and let it revert that hunk automatically
questions.explanation: git revert inverts the whole commit, so it would also remove the fee fix and the rename that other services now depend on. The commit was not atomic, which is why it cannot be cheaply undone. reset --hard on a shared branch destroys history for everyone, and bisect only locates a commit; it never edits one.

questions.question: Which of these commits fails the 'complete' test of atomicity even though it does exactly one thing?
options: A commit that renames a method and updates all twenty of its callers across six files in one change
A commit that adds a bug fix together with the regression test that demonstrates the fix
A commit that adds a class the next commit will wire in, with an import that fails compilation
A commit that reformats a single test file with the formatter and changes no behaviour at all
questions.explanation: Complete means the tree builds and passes at that commit. A commit that does not compile cannot be bisected through and cannot base a hotfix. The rename with its callers is one logical change across many files; the fix plus its test is one change because neither is complete without the other; the reformat is self-contained.

questions.question: In Conventional Commits, which subject line is well-formed for this course and under 72 characters?
options: feat(phase-00/04): git-for-engineers
Added the git lesson for phase 0 lesson 4.
feat: Added Git For Engineers lesson and fixed the audit script and README
FEAT(phase-00/04) - git-for-engineers
questions.explanation: type(scope): description, lower-case imperative, no trailing period. The second option has no type and uses past tense; the third uses past tense, mixes three changes with 'and', and has no scope; the fourth capitalises the type and uses a dash instead of a colon.

questions.question: git bisect is searching 1,000 commits between a known-good tag and HEAD. About how many build-and-test steps does it need, and what breaks the arithmetic?
options: About 500 steps; a merge commit anywhere in the range doubles the count
About 10 steps; a commit in the range that does not compile forces a skip and can leave the culprit ambiguous
About 32 steps; a commit that touches more than one file makes bisect test each file separately
About 1,000 steps; bisect must check out every commit because tests are not monotone
questions.explanation: Bisect is binary search: ceil(log2(1000)) = 10 steps. The precondition is a monotone good/bad predicate, so a commit that cannot be built cannot be classified; git bisect skip moves to a neighbour, and a run of such commits leaves an unresolvable range. Merges and file counts do not change the log2 bound.

questions.question: You are mid-lesson with a warm build in code/java/.out and must ship a hotfix from main. Which approach leaves the lesson directory untouched and needs no stash?
options: git stash -u, git switch main, fix, git switch -, git stash pop
git worktree add ../hotfix main, fix and commit there, git worktree remove ../hotfix
git clone the repository a second time into ../hotfix and push from the clone
git commit -am wip on the lesson branch, switch to main, fix, then git reset --soft
questions.explanation: A worktree is a second working directory on the same .git store with its own branch, index, and untracked files, so nothing in the lesson checkout moves. Stash with -u works but risks a conflicting pop and drops the build output; a second clone duplicates objects and refs and loses local branches; a wip commit pollutes history and reset is the wrong tool.

questions.question: What belongs in the body of a lesson commit in this course, and what must never be in the commit at all?
options: Body: a list of every file changed; never: the docs/en.md, which is regenerated by build_catalog.py
Body: the why, rejected alternatives, and an Evidence line with command, exit code, and counts; never: .out/, catalog.json, __pycache__, or *-LEARNING.md
Body: the full diff summary from git diff --stat; never: the quiz.json, which lives in a separate repository
Body: the reviewer's name and the sprint number; never: README.md or ROADMAP.md, which contributors must not touch
questions.explanation: The body says what the diff cannot: the reason and what was verified. Generated and personal files (.out/, catalog.json, __pycache__/, *-LEARNING.md) are gitignored and never committed. docs/en.md and quiz.json are the lesson itself and are always committed; README.md and ROADMAP.md are regenerated by build_catalog.py and may be committed alongside the lesson.
